items.title: The U.S. product
items.text: Production ended on October 10, 2008. Distributors were asked to fill the space with Sparks.[^14][^15]

items.title: The limited releases
items.text: Sold from the July 4 weekend to Labor Day in 2017 and again from May 2018, with 20% more made the second time. MillerCoors did not publish the size of either run. There was no release in 2019.[^24][^26][^28]

items.title: Japan
items.text: Sold by Coors’s Japanese subsidiary from the late 1990s until shipments stopped at the end of 2021. Hakutsuru Sake Brewing relaunched it on March 31, 2023 at ¥298 a bottle before tax. The brand’s Japanese site, zima.jp, was online when we checked in October 2026.[^7][^30][^31]

items.title: The U.S. trademark
items.text: Molson Coors let its registration expire in 2024 while Retrobrands, a company that revives old brands, was seeking to cancel it and register the name itself. The outcome of that application is not in our sources.[^32]

items.title: The owner
items.text: Adolph Coors Company became Molson Coors in 2005 and put its U.S. business into MillerCoors in 2008.[^11]

items.title: The idea
items.text: U.S. off-premise sales of hard seltzer reached about $1.5 billion in 2019, up from $496 million the year before.[^35]

blocks.title: Who has owned or sold the name
blocks.subtitle: The brand was never sold. Its owner changed shape around it three times.

nodes.what: Introduces Zima in three test markets and sets up the Zima Beverage Company as an operating unit in Memphis.[^1][^33]
Formed by the merger of Adolph Coors Company and Molson Inc. on February 9, 2005.[^11]
The U.S. joint venture of Molson Coors and SABMiller takes over the brand at home. Molson Coors keeps Japan.[^11]
Exclusive import and sales agreement with Molson Coors for Zima and Blue Moon in Japan.[^31]
Molson Coors lets the U.S. mark lapse. Retrobrands has applied for it.[^32]
